*   **Order of Operations:** Applying depth cueing before shading distorts gradient vectors, leading to incorrect shading if not adjusted [S1, S2, unofficial].

The claim states that applying depth cueing before shading distorts gradient vectors, leading to incorrect shading if not adjusted. Source [S1] explicitly states: 'Otherwise, distortion by the depth cueing would result in incorrect gradient vector by which the shading effect is computed.' It further explains that to work around this, one can reverse the order (apply depth cueing first) and 'adjust the result to get the desired effect.' This confirms that the distortion occurs and requires adjustment.

Source [S1] explicitly states: 'In this paper, we have shown that other O n3 spatial domain rendering computations that arise in volume rendering (i.e., shading and depth cueing) can be replaced with O n2 frequency domain methods'. The reversed order approximation may introduce errors if not adjusted, particularly when $V \cdot L \neq 0$ [S1, S2, unofficial].

The evidence in both Source [S1] and Source [S2] explicitly states that reversing the order of shading and depth cueing introduces a 'difference term' (error) proportional to the dot product of the view direction V and light direction L (V • L). Both sources confirm that if V • L is not zero, an adjustment is necessary to correct this error, although they note that for common cases where L is perpendicular to V, the term is zero and no adjustment is needed. Thus, the claim that errors may be introduced if not adjusted, particularly when V • L ≠ 0, is fully supported by the text.
supported

Combined Depth Cueing and Shading is a frequency-domain volume rendering technique that integrates linear attenuation (depth cueing) and hemispherical directional shading into a single rendering pass [S1, S2, unofficial].

The claim states that Combined Depth Cueing and Shading is a frequency-domain volume rendering technique integrating linear attenuation (depth cueing) and hemispherical directional shading into a single rendering pass. Source [S1] explicitly discusses combining these techniques in the frequency domain. It mentions applying linear depth cueing with respect to the observer's position and using a hemispherical light source for directional shading. Furthermore, it describes a method to reverse the order of operations to apply depth cueing and interpolation simultaneously using a composite filter, effectively integrating them into the rendering process (a pass). The evidence supports all specific details mentioned in the claim.

The gradient term of the shading equation is affected by the order reversal [S1, S2, unofficial].

The evidence explicitly states in both Source [S1] and Source [S2] that when the order of shading and depth cueing is reversed, the gradient term of the shading equation is affected. Specifically, the text notes: 'We focus on the gradient term of the shading equation... since other terms are not affected by the order.' It further explains that reversing the order introduces a 'difference term' (an error term) into the gradient calculation, which must be adjusted for unless the light direction is perpendicular to the view direction.

*   **When to Use:** When real-time or near-real-time rendering of large volumes is required, and occlusion is not critical [S1, S2, unofficial].

The claim states that the technique is used when real-time or near-real-time rendering of large volumes is required and occlusion is not critical. Source [S1] explicitly mentions that the frequency domain approach has a 'speed advantage' allowing a 128^3 volume to be rendered in a 'fraction of a second' and suggests it can achieve 'interactive rendering'. It also notes that the projection operator is 'nonoccluding, resulting in a loss of realism' but that the shading techniques help restore realism. This aligns perfectly with the claim's conditions: high speed (real-time/near-real-time) and the trade-off regarding occlusion.
